mainTopic: Upper and lower residents of one house: the tenant's rights after a collapse, who supplies the ceiling and plaster, who fixes leaking water, and rebuilding a collapsed house.
overview: The amud opens with a chain of questions about a tenant whose rented upper story collapsed and who moved down into the owner's house. Does he live there alone or share it? Does he enter through the doors or by way of the roof? If there are two upper stories and the lower one breaks, must he climb to the top one? Each question asks what the tenant agreed to when he rented, and all of them end in תיקו. Next the גמרא explains the word תקרה (ceiling) in רבי יוסי's ruling: mats and beams, or wide planks, each following local building custom. It then brings a case of broken floor plaster that let water drip downstairs, where two אמוראים argue whether the upper or the lower resident must repair it. The גמרא first tries to tie their argument to רבי יוסי and the רבנן in our משנה, but the tree-and-pit משנה shows that cannot work. So it ties the אמוראים to the tree-and-pit dispute, and explains that our משנה argues about what the plaster is for: strengthening the ceiling or leveling the floor. Finally a new משנה teaches that when a house and its upper story collapse, the upper owner may rebuild and live downstairs until repaid, while רבי יהודה says he must first rebuild both floors so he owes no rent.

steps.title: Does the tenant live downstairs alone or together with the owner?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the upper-story tenant, now moved downstairs, takes the house for himself or shares it with the owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: When the tenant moves downstairs, does he live there alone, the way he lived alone upstairs? Or do both of them live there, because the owner can say: 'I did not rent to you so that I would be pushed out of my own home'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is asking a question about the משנה's ruling that the tenant moves down into the owner's house: does the owner have to leave, or do they share?
steps.deeperAnalysis: One side says the tenant had a place all to himself before, so he should have a place all to himself now. The other side says the owner never agreed to be thrown out of his own home, so at most the tenant shares it with him.

keyTerms.meaning: just like at the beginning (the way things were originally)
or perhaps (opens the other side of a question)
with the intention of / on the understanding that
to take me out (to push me out)

phrases.aramaic: כְּשֶׁהוּא דָּר, לְבַדּוֹ הוּא דָּר כִּדְמֵעִיקָּרָא,
phrases.english: When he lives there, does he live alone, just as at the beginning,
phrases.notes: "He" is the upper-story tenant who moved down into the owner's house, as the משנה allowed.

phrases.english: or perhaps both of them live there,
because he (the owner) says to him:
"I did not rent to you with the intention that I be pushed out."

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּשֶׁהוּא דָּר, לְבַדּוֹ הוּא דָּר כִּדְמֵעִיקָּרָא, אוֹ דִלְמָא שְׁנֵיהֶם דָּרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the גמרא's questions about the משנה's rule that the tenant moves downstairs.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Must the owner leave his house to the tenant, or do they live there together?

steps.title: If they share, does the tenant enter through the door or by way of the roof?
steps.stepSummary: Assuming they share the house, the גמרא asks whether the tenant may use the regular entrances or must still climb up and come down through the roof.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say that both of them live there, how does the tenant come and go? Through the doors, or by way of the roof? Do we say: just like at the beginning, when he went by way of the roof, so now too he goes by way of the roof? Or perhaps he can say: 'I agreed to climb up. I never agreed to climb up and then climb down.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא builds a second question on top of the first: if the tenant shares the house, does he walk in like the owner, or must he still use the roof route?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner's side: the tenant always reached his home by going up to the roof, so let him keep doing that. The tenant's side: he only agreed to the effort of going up, and going up to the roof and then down into the house is a burden he never accepted.

keyTerms.meaning: if you will say (if we decide the earlier question this way)
by way of the entrances (the doors)
I accepted upon myself (I agreed to)

steps.confusionAlert: Here the word עלייה means "going up" (an ascent). Elsewhere in this סוגיא it means an upper story. Watch which meaning fits.

phrases.aramaic: אִם תִּמְצָא לוֹמַר שְׁנֵיהֶם דָּרִין בּוֹ,
phrases.english: If you say that both of them live in it,
when he uses it, does he use it by way of the entrances,
or does he use it by way of the roofs?
Does he (the owner) say: just as at the beginning,
just as at the beginning it was by way of the roofs,
now too it is by way of the roofs.
Or perhaps he (the tenant) can say to him:
"Going up, I accepted upon myself;
going up and coming down, I did not accept upon myself."

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם תִּמְצָא לוֹמַר שְׁנֵיהֶם דָּרִין בּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Assumes the answer "they share" to step 1 and asks a further question.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the tenant held to his original route through the roof, or may he use the doors because he never agreed to go up and then down?

steps.title: Two upper stories: if the lower one breaks, must he climb to the top?
steps.stepSummary: Assuming the tenant only agreed to climb up, the גמרא asks about a building with two upper stories where the lower one collapses.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say the tenant can say 'I did not agree to go up and come down,' what about two upper stories, one on top of the other? If the top one broke, he simply goes down and lives in the lower one. But if the lower one broke, must he go up all the way and live in the top one?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא builds a third question on the second. It sets up a new case: two upper stories stacked on each other, where the lower one breaks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the upper one breaks, it is obvious he moves down, since that is easier. The question is only when the lower one breaks: living in the top story means climbing two levels, which is more than he originally did.

keyTerms.meaning: one on top of the other
the upper one / the lower one
to go up all the way

phrases.aramaic: אִם תִּמְצָא לוֹמַר, מָצֵי אֲמַר לֵיהּ:
phrases.english: If you say that he can say to him:
"Going up and coming down I did not accept upon myself,"

phrases.aramaic: שְׁתֵּי עֲלִיּוֹת זוֹ עַל גַּב זוֹ, מַהוּ?
phrases.english: then with two upper stories, one on top of the other, what is the law?
If the upper one broke, he goes down and lives in the lower one.
If the lower one broke,
what is the law: must he go up all the way into the upper one?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם תִּמְצָא לוֹמַר, מָצֵי אֲמַר לֵיהּ: עֲלִיָּיה וִירִידָה לָא קַבֵּילִי עֲלַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Assumes the tenant's side wins in step 2 and moves on to a new case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: When the lower of two upper stories breaks, must the tenant move to the top story?

steps.title: The two sides: did he agree to "an upper story" or to just one flight up?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא lays out the two ways to look at the two-story case: what exactly did the tenant agree to when he rented?
steps.simpleTranslation: Do we say the owner can tell him: 'You agreed to the name "upper story," and the top floor is also an upper story'? Or perhaps the tenant agreed to climb one level, not two?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the two sides of the question it just asked about two stacked upper stories.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner's side reads the rental as "an upper story," any upper story. The tenant's side reads it as one specific amount of climbing, one level. Both sides hang on how we understand what the tenant agreed to.

phrases.english: Do we say that he (the owner) can say to him:
"You accepted upon yourself the name 'upper story'"?

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא: חַד עֲלִיָּיה – קַבֵּיל עֲלֵיהּ,
phrases.english: Or perhaps: one going-up he accepted upon himself,
but two going-ups he did not accept upon himself?
phrases.notes: Here עליות means "climbs," not "upper stories." He agreed to climb one level, not two.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי אָמְרִינַן דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ: שֵׁם עֲלִיָּיה קַבֵּילְיתְּ עֲלָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the two possible answers to the question in step 3.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Did the tenant agree to the general idea of "an upper story" or to a specific amount of climbing?

steps.title: The questions remain unanswered
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא ends the chain of questions with תיקו: they stay unresolved.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says תיקו, meaning no answer was found, so these questions stay open.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No source settles these questions, so the גמרא leaves them standing without a decision. Only the משנה's basic rule is certain: if the floor breaks and the owner won't fix it, the tenant moves downstairs.

keyTerms.meaning: let it stand (the question stays unresolved)

steps.whatToRemember: These questions build on one another, and each asks what the tenant agreed to when he rented: his own space, the roof route, one climb or any upper story. None is decided; they end in תיקו.

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.triggerLanguage: תֵּיקוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the whole chain of questions without an answer.

steps.title: What does 'ceiling' mean in רבי יוסי's ruling?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי יוסי's line in the משנה and asks what the word תקרה (ceiling) refers to.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי says: The lower one provides the ceiling, and so on. What is meant by 'ceiling'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to a line in the משנה and asks what one word in it means. This sets up the answers that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי splits the repair costs: the lower owner gives the ceiling and the upper owner gives the plaster. To know what each person pays for, we first need to know exactly which building materials count as the 'ceiling'.

keyTerms.meaning: the lower one (owner of the ground floor)
'etc.': the quote from the משנה continues

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says:
The lower one provides the ceiling, etc.
What is 'ceiling'?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי ״תִּקְרָה״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the תיקו on the tenant questions, the גמרא moves on to the next line of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which building materials the word תקרה refers to in רבי יוסי's ruling.

steps.title: Two definitions of 'ceiling'
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי בר חנינא says the ceiling means mats and beams. ריש לקיש says it means wide wooden planks.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי בר חנינא says: mats and beams. יוסטיני says in the name of רבי שמעון בן לקיש: wide wooden planks.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים give two different answers to what 'ceiling' means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One opinion describes a ceiling made of reed mats laid on beams. The other describes a ceiling made of wide planks. Either way, these are the parts the lower owner must supply.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina says:
Mats and beams.

phrases.aramaic: וְ[יוּ]סְטִינִי אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ:
phrases.english: And Yustini says that Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish says:
phrases.notes: Some versions read the name as סטיני; the letters in square brackets are the corrected wording.

phrases.english: Wide wooden planks.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Either mats with beams, or wide wooden planks.

steps.title: No real argument: each follows his local custom
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the two opinions do not really disagree. Each one describes how ceilings were built in his own place.
steps.simpleTranslation: And they do not disagree. One Sage spoke according to his place, and the other Sage spoke according to his place.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the two definitions are not a real argument. Each Sage was describing what a ceiling looked like where he lived.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The law is the same for both: the lower owner provides whatever a ceiling is made of. Only the building style differs from place to place.

keyTerms.meaning: this Sage according to his place (its local custom)

phrases.english: And they do not disagree:

phrases.aramaic: מָר כִּי אַתְרֵיהּ וּמָר כִּי אַתְרֵיהּ.
phrases.english: This Sage according to his place, and this Sage according to his place.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא פְּלִיגִי: מָר כִּי אַתְרֵיהּ וּמָר כִּי אַתְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Settles the apparent disagreement of step 7.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The 'ceiling' is whatever local builders use for it. The two definitions only reflect different local customs.
steps.whatToRemember: Different answers do not always mean an argument. Sometimes each Sage is describing what was normal in his own place.

steps.title: Broken floor plaster: water leaks from upstairs to downstairs
steps.stepSummary: Two people lived in one house, one upstairs and one downstairs. The floor plaster broke, so water from upstairs leaked down. Who must fix it?
steps.simpleTranslation: There were two people living in a house, one upstairs and one downstairs. The floor plaster broke. When the upper one washed with water, it ran down and damaged the lower one. Who has to repair it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real case and asks who must pay for the repair. This sets up the argument that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The upper resident's water is doing the damage, but it lands in the lower resident's space. The question is whether the one causing the harm fixes it, or the one being harmed protects himself.

keyTerms.meaning: plaster layer on top of the ceiling, which forms the upstairs floor

phrases.english: There were these two people who were living [in one house],
one upstairs and one downstairs.
The plaster broke.
When the upper one would wash with water,
it would run down and damage the lower one.
Who repairs it?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנְהוּ בֵּי תְרֵי דַּהֲווֹ דָּיְירִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new case that is connected to the משנה's topic of upper and lower stories.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the upstairs or the downstairs resident must repair the broken plaster.

steps.title: Two אמוראים argue over who repairs
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא בר אבא says the upper resident repairs. רבי אלעי, quoting רבי חייא בן רבי יוסי, says the lower resident repairs. A פסוק about יוסף helps us remember who said what.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא בר אבא says: the upper one repairs. רבי אלעי says in the name of רבי חייא בן רבי יוסי: the lower one repairs. A memory aid: 'And יוסף was brought down to מצרים.'
steps.whatsHappening: Two answers are given to the question, along with a memory trick for remembering which Sage said which.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two opinions are complete opposites. The memory aid connects 'יוסף' to רבי חייא, son of רבי יוסי, and 'brought down' to the lower resident. So the son of רבי יוסי is the one who says the downstairs resident repairs.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up רבי חייא בר אבא with רבי חייא בְּרַבִּי יוסי. They are two different people holding opposite views.

phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba says:
The upper one repairs it,

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבִּי אִלְעַי מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי חִיָּיא בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי אָמַר:
phrases.english: and Rabbi Elai says in the name of Rabbi Ḥiyya, son of Rabbi Yosei:
The lower one repairs it.
And a memory aid: 'And Joseph was brought down to Egypt.'
phrases.notes: בראשית 39:1. 'יוסף' hints at the son of רבי יוסי, and 'brought down' hints at the lower one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the two rulings on the question of step 9.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי חייא בר אבא says the upper resident repairs. רבי חייא בן רבי יוסי (quoted by רבי אלעי) says the lower resident repairs.

steps.title: Is this the same argument as רבי יוסי and the רבנן?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the two אמוראים are arguing about the same idea as רבי יוסי and the רבנן: is the damager or the damaged person responsible for keeping away?
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say that רבי חייא בר אבא and רבי אלעי are arguing about the same thing as רבי יוסי and the רבנן? The one who says the upper one repairs holds that the damager must keep himself away from the one he damages. The one who says the lower one repairs holds that the damaged person must keep himself away from the damager.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proposes linking the new argument to the older argument in the משנה, based on a general principle about damages.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proposed principle is this: either the one causing harm must take steps to stop it (so the upper resident repairs), or the one at risk must protect himself (so the lower resident repairs). In our משנה, רבי יוסי makes the upper owner provide the plaster, which fits the first view.

keyTerms.meaning: shall we say? (a suggestion the גמרא may later reject)

steps.whyThisMatters: Whether the damager or the damaged person must keep away is a basic question in the laws of neighbors.

phrases.aramaic: לֵימָא רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא וְרַבִּי אִלְעַי
phrases.english: Shall we say that Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Elai
disagree about the dispute of Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis?
According to the one who says the upper one repairs,
he holds that it is on the damager
to distance himself from the one damaged.
And the one who says the lower one repairs,
he holds that it is on the one damaged
to distance himself from the damager.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵימָא רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא וְרַבִּי אִלְעַי בִּפְלוּגְתָּא דְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי וְרַבָּנַן קָמִיפַּלְגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to explain the dispute of step 10 by tying it to the משנה's dispute.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the dispute between the אמוראים is the same as the תנאים' dispute about who must distance himself from damage.

steps.title: But we know רבי יוסי and the רבנן hold the opposite
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the suggestion: elsewhere, רבי יוסי and the רבנן seem to hold the reverse positions on damages.
steps.simpleTranslation: Can you really think that רבי יוסי and the רבנן argue about damages here? But we have heard them say the opposite!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the suggestion from step 11, claiming another source shows these תנאים holding the opposite views.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the suggestion were right, רבי יוסי would hold that the damager must keep away. But another משנה seems to show the reverse. The גמרא is about to quote that source.

keyTerms.meaning: and can you really think so?

phrases.english: And can you understand it that way?

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי וְרַבָּנַן לְעִנְיַן נְזָקִין פְּלִיגִי?
phrases.english: Do Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis disagree about damages [here]?
But we have heard them say the opposite,

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתִיסְבְּרָא רַבִּי יוֹסֵי וְרַבָּנַן לְעִנְיַן נְזָקִין פְּלִיגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the link proposed in step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 11 that רבי יוסי holds the damager must distance himself.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In another source these תנאים take the reverse positions on who must distance himself, so the proposed link cannot be right.

steps.title: The משנה of the tree and the pit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה: a tree must be kept 25 cubits from a pit (50 for a carob or sycamore). Who must give way depends on which one was there first.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned: One must keep a tree 25 cubits away from a pit, and a carob or sycamore 50 cubits, whether it is above or to the side. If the pit came first, he cuts down the tree and pays its value. If the tree came first, he does not cut it down. If it is unclear which came first, he does not cut it down.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the source behind its challenge. This is the anonymous first opinion of a משנה about trees and pits, and the גמרא will go on to show where רבי יוסי stands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Tree roots damage a pit, so the tree is the damager. In this opinion the tree owner, the damager, must keep away, but only if the pit was there first. This sets up the contrast showing which side holds the damager responsible.

keyTerms.meaning: as we learned in a משנה

phrases.english: As we learned in a mishna:
One must distance a tree from a pit
twenty-five cubits,
and with a carob or sycamore, fifty cubits,
whether above or to the side.
If the pit came first,
he cuts down [the tree] and pays its value.
If the tree came first, he may not cut it down.

phrases.aramaic: סָפֵק זֶה קָדַם סָפֵק זֶה קָדַם –
phrases.english: If it is uncertain whether this came first or that came first,
he may not cut it down.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּתְנַן: מַרְחִיקִין אֶת הָאִילָן מִן הַבּוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source that backs up the challenge in step 12.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יוסי and the רבנן hold views on damages that are the reverse of what step 11 assumed.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה about distancing a tree from a pit, whose first opinion makes the tree owner (the damager) distance himself.

steps.title: רבי יוסי's view in the tree-and-pit case
steps.stepSummary: The quoted משנה continues: רבי יוסי says the tree owner does not have to cut down his tree, even if the pit was there first, because each person is using his own land.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי says: Even if the pit was there before the tree, the tree owner does not cut it down. This person digs in his own land, and that person plants in his own land.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps quoting the same משנה from the last step and brings in רבי יוסי's opinion. This sets up the challenge that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first part of the משנה (the רבנן) said the tree must be cut down if the pit came first. רבי יוסי disagrees: each owner may do as he likes in his own property. So the tree owner does not have to move away from the pit.

keyTerms.meaning: he does not cut down (the tree)

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says:

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהַבּוֹר קוֹדֶמֶת לָאִילָן –
phrases.english: Even though the pit came before the tree,
he does not cut it down,
because this one digs within his own property,
and that one plants within his own property.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהַבּוֹר קוֹדֶמֶת לָאִילָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes quoting the משנה begun in step 13.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יוסי does not require the potential damager (the tree owner) to move away.
steps.raayaSupportSource: משנה in בבא בתרא about a tree near a pit.

steps.title: So the positions are the reverse of what was suggested
steps.stepSummary: From the tree-and-pit משנה, the גמרא concludes that רבי יוסי puts the burden on the damaged person and the רבנן put it on the damager. That is the opposite of the earlier suggestion.
steps.simpleTranslation: So it seems that רבי יוסי holds the damaged person must keep himself away, and the רבנן hold the damager must keep himself away!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws the conclusion from the משנה it just quoted. That conclusion completes the challenge against the suggestion in step 11.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 tried to read our משנה about upstairs and downstairs residents as the same issue of damager and damaged. But the tree-and-pit משנה shows how רבי יוסי and the רבנן really hold on that issue, and it doesn't fit how they rule in our משנה. So the suggested link falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: the one who causes the damage
to keep himself at a distance

phrases.english: Apparently, Rabbi Yosei holds
it is on the damaged one to keep himself away,
and the Rabbis hold
it is on the damager to keep himself away!

steps.whatToRemember: In the tree-and-pit case, רבי יוסי says the damaged person must keep away, and the רבנן say the damager must keep away.
steps.triggerLanguage: אַלְמָא, רַבִּי יוֹסֵי סָבַר עַל הַנִּיזָּק לְהַרְחִיק אֶת עַצְמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the משנה quoted in steps 13-14.
steps.kashyaTarget: The suggestion in step 11 that the אמוראים follow the dispute of רבי יוסי and the רבנן in our משנה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The tree-and-pit משנה shows each תנא's real view on damager and damaged. That view doesn't match their rulings in our משנה, so our משנה can't be about that issue.

steps.title: The אמוראים follow the tree-and-pit dispute instead
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes its approach. If the two אמוראים do argue about damager versus damaged, they follow the dispute of רבי יוסי and the רבנן in the tree-and-pit case, not in our משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, if you want to say they argue about this idea, they argue along the lines of the dispute of רבי יוסי and the רבנן there.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives up linking the אמוראים to our משנה. It links them to the tree-and-pit משנה instead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea of a damager-versus-damaged argument stays, but its source moves. The upper resident is like the damager and the lower resident is like the damaged one, so each אמורא can follow one side of the tree-and-pit dispute. The next two steps explain what the רבנן and רבי יוסי of our משנה are really arguing about.

phrases.english: Rather, if one can say they disagree,
phrases.notes: "They" means the two אמוראים from step 10, רבי חייא בר אבא and רבי אלעי.

phrases.english: in the dispute of Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis
of there they disagree.
phrases.notes: "There" means the tree-and-pit case just quoted.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אִי אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר פְּלִיגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 15 by moving the link to a different dispute.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-anchoring: the same argument is linked to a different תנאים dispute.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The אמוראים follow the dispute of רבי יוסי and the רבנן in our משנה about the upper and lower residents.
steps.terutzMaskana: If they argue about damager versus damaged at all, they follow the tree-and-pit dispute.

steps.title: Then what is our משנה arguing about?
steps.stepSummary: If our משנה is not about damager versus damaged, what is the real point of the argument between רבי יוסי and the רבנן here?
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוסי and the רבנן here, what are they arguing about?
steps.whatsHappening: Now that the old explanation is gone, the גמרא asks what the dispute in our משנה is really about. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our משנה still has a dispute about who supplies the plaster. Since it can't be explained as damager versus damaged, the גמרא needs a new reason behind each opinion.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis of here,
about what do they disagree?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי וְרַבָּנַן דְּהָכָא, בְּמַאי פְּלִיגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from step 16: if our משנה is not about damager versus damaged, its dispute needs a new explanation.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The real reason behind the dispute in our משנה about who supplies the plaster.

steps.title: They argue about what the plaster is for
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן hold that plaster strengthens the ceiling, so the lower resident supplies it. רבי יוסי holds that plaster fills in holes to level the floor, so the upper resident supplies it.
steps.simpleTranslation: They argue about strengthening the ceiling. The רבנן hold the plaster is there to strengthen the ceiling, and the lower resident has to strengthen the ceiling. רבי יוסי holds the plaster is there to level out holes, and leveling out holes is the upper resident's job.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the argument is about what the plaster does. Whoever benefits from that job has to pay for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the plaster is part of the ceiling's strength, it belongs to the ceiling, and the lower resident must keep his ceiling strong. If the plaster only smooths out holes in the floor, it serves the person walking on it, the upper resident. This has nothing to do with who is the damager.

keyTerms.meaning: the plaster layer on top of the ceiling boards
the lower resident / the upper resident

phrases.english: They disagree about the strength of the ceiling.
The Rabbis hold:
the plaster is for strengthening the ceiling,
and strengthening the ceiling
the lower resident needs to strengthen.
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the words in round brackets. Either way, it means the lower resident has to do it.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yosei holds:
the plaster is for leveling out holes,
and leveling out holes is on the upper resident to level.
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the words in round brackets. The meaning is still that leveling the floor is the upper resident's job.

steps.whatToRemember: In our משנה, the argument is about what the plaster does. The רבנן say it strengthens the ceiling, so the lower resident supplies it. רבי יוסי says it levels the floor, so the upper resident supplies it.
steps.triggerLanguage: בְּחוֹזֶק תִּקְרָה קָמִיפַּלְגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The dispute is about what the plaster is for: strengthening the ceiling (lower resident) or leveling holes (upper resident).

steps.title: רב אשי: רבי יוסי agrees when the damage is like his own arrows
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer from step 16. רב אשי reported that in רב כהנא's study hall they said רבי יוסי agrees the damager is responsible when the damage comes like his own arrows.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But רב אשי said: When we were in רב כהנא's study hall, we used to say that רבי יוסי agrees in a case of his own arrows!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions whether the אמוראים can really be following the tree-and-pit dispute. It quotes a teaching that limits רבי יוסי's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 16 assumed that one אמורא could follow רבי יוסי and free the upper resident. But if רבי יוסי agrees that a person is responsible for damage that goes out from him like shooting arrows, then water flowing down from the upper resident may count as his own 'arrows.' If so, even רבי יוסי would hold the upper resident responsible.

keyTerms.meaning: his own arrows: damage that goes out directly from a person

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יוסי has not changed his view that the damaged person must keep away. רב אשי says that view has a limit: when the damage goes out from the person like arrows he shoots, even רבי יוסי makes the damager responsible.

phrases.english: Is that so? But didn't Rav Ashi say:
When I was in the study hall of Rav Kahana,
we used to say:
Rabbi Yosei agrees in the case of his own arrows!
phrases.notes: "His arrows" means damage that goes straight out from a person, like an arrow he shoots.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינִי? וְהָאָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to challenge the answer of step 16 after the side explanation in steps 17-18.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 16 that the אמוראים follow the tree-and-pit dispute of רבי יוסי and the רבנן.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוסי agrees that a person is responsible for damage that goes out from him like arrows. Leaking water may be like that, so no אמורא could use רבי יוסי to free the upper resident.

steps.title: The water stops first and only then drips down
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the challenge: in our case the water does not fall directly. It pools first and only later drips down, so it is not 'his own arrows.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The case is where the water stops, and afterward it falls.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 19. The water does not drop straight down. It first stops on the upper floor and only later drips through.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 19, רבי יוסי admitted that the damager pays when the damage comes like his own arrows, meaning straight from his action. The גמרא explains that here the water first comes to rest and only then flows to the hole and falls. Because of that pause, the damage is only indirect, so the answer from step 16 still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: They stop / come to a halt

steps.whatToRemember: The upper resident is not seen as directly causing the damage, because the water pauses before it falls. This lets the earlier explanation of רבי יוסי stand.

phrases.english: Where the water stops, and afterward falls.
phrases.notes: This is the water used upstairs. It runs along the floor, rests, and only later drips through a hole that is not right under where it was poured.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּפָסְקִי מַיָּא וַהֲדַר נָפְלִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 19 by narrowing the case so it is not 'his own arrows.'
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (the water pauses before it falls)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Water dripping from the upper floor seems to be direct damage, like the upper resident's own arrows, which רבי יוסי agrees he must pay for.
steps.terutzMaskana: The water comes to rest first and only then falls, so the damage is indirect. רבי יוסי's view that the damaged person must protect himself still applies.

steps.title: New משנה: the upper owner may rebuild the house and live in it until repaid
steps.stepSummary: A house and the upper story above it belong to two people, and both collapsed. If the lower owner refuses to rebuild, the upper owner builds the lower house and lives in it until he is repaid.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: A house and an upper story belong to two people, and they collapsed. The upper owner told the house owner to build, and he does not want to build. The upper owner may build the house and live in it until the house owner pays him his expenses.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins with a new case. The upper story cannot be rebuilt without the lower house under it, so the משנה lets the upper owner build the lower house and live there until he is paid back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The upper owner has a right to his upper story, but it needs the lower house to rest on. If the lower owner refuses to build, the upper owner may do it himself. Until his costs are repaid, he lives in the lower house he built. This is the view of the תנא קמא.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
A house and an upper story belonging to two people that collapsed,

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר בַּעַל הָעֲלִיָּיה לְבַעַל הַבַּיִת לִבְנוֹת
phrases.english: the upper-story owner told the house owner to build,
and he does not want to build,

phrases.aramaic: הֲרֵי בַּעַל הָעֲלִיָּיה בּוֹנֶה אֶת הַבַּיִת
phrases.english: then the upper-story owner builds the house
and lives inside it,
until the other gives him his expenses.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הַבַּיִת וְהָעֲלִיָּיה שֶׁל שְׁנַיִם שֶׁנָּפְלוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the dripping-water discussion is finished.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the lower owner refuses to rebuild, the upper owner may rebuild the lower house and live in it until his expenses are repaid.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: living in the house needs rent, so build both floors first
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה objects that living in someone else's house requires paying rent. Instead, the upper owner builds both floors, roofs the upper one, and then lives downstairs until repaid.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: This person too is living in his friend's property, so he must pay him rent. Rather, the upper owner builds the house and the upper story, roofs the upper one, and lives in the house until the other pays him his expenses.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה disagrees with the first opinion in the משנה. He gives a different way for the upper owner to get his money back without owing rent.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה worries that if the upper owner lives in the lower house, he is getting free use of another person's home, which would be like interest on the money he is owed. So he says the upper owner should first rebuild his own upper story too. Once he has his own place to live, staying downstairs gives him no extra benefit, so he owes no rent.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי יהודה does not deny that the upper owner can rebuild and be repaid. He only changes how it is done, so that the upper owner never gets free benefit from someone else's house.
steps.whyThisMatters: This dispute sets up the coming גמרא discussion about why staying in the house would count as a forbidden benefit, which is connected to the laws of interest.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:

phrases.aramaic: אַף זֶה דָּר בְּתוֹךְ שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ,
phrases.english: This one too is living inside his fellow's property,
so he must pay him rent.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא בַּעַל הָעֲלִיָּיה בּוֹנֶה אֶת הַבַּיִת וְאֶת הָעֲלִיָּיה,
phrases.english: Rather, the upper-story owner builds the house and the upper story,
and roofs the upper one,
phrases.notes: The וּ in square brackets is added in the corrected wording, so read it as 'and roofs.'

phrases.english: and he lives in the house
until the other gives him his expenses.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: אַף זֶה דָּר בְּתוֹךְ שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the first opinion in the משנה (step 21) and gives a different procedure.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Living in the lower house would require rent. So the upper owner must rebuild and roof both floors, and then he may live downstairs until he is repaid.
